lesson.title: One Lone Pair, One Pyramid: Ammonia's Shape
lesson.summary: Trigonal pyramidal geometry is what a tetrahedral electron arrangement looks like once the lone pair is left out of the naming, an umbrella shaped molecule best illustrated by ammonia and central to its behavior as a base.
lesson.body:
Trigonal pyramidal geometry arises from a steric number of four with exactly one lone pair, written in shorthand as AX3E. The electron geometry underneath is tetrahedral, the same four domain arrangement that produces methane's perfectly symmetric shape when all four domains are bonding pairs. But when one of those four domains is a lone pair instead, naming only the visible atoms, the central atom plus the three atoms it is bonded to, produces a different shape: a tripod like pyramid with the central atom at the apex and the three bonded atoms forming the base.

Ammonia, NH3, is the essential example. Nitrogen has five valence electrons, three of which form bonding pairs to three hydrogen atoms, leaving one lone pair on nitrogen. That gives a steric number of four, tetrahedral electron geometry, and since one of the four domains is a lone pair rather than a bonding pair, the molecular geometry, describing only the positions of the four atoms, nitrogen and three hydrogens, is trigonal pyramidal. This connects directly back to the lone pairs concept: the lone pair is not shown in the pyramid shape itself, but it still occupies real space and still repels its neighbors exactly as VSEPR predicts.

That invisible lone pair has a very visible effect on the measured bond angle. The ideal tetrahedral angle is 109.5 degrees, but the actual H to N to H bond angle in ammonia is about 107 degrees, noticeably compressed. The explanation is the same one that applies throughout VSEPR theory: a lone pair is attracted to only one nucleus rather than two, so its electron cloud spreads out more broadly than a bonding pair's cloud does, and that extra spread pushes the three N to H bonding domains closer together than a perfectly symmetric tetrahedral arrangement would allow.

Lining up methane, ammonia, and water side by side makes this compression trend impossible to miss. Methane, with zero lone pairs on its central carbon, keeps the full ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees. Ammonia, with one lone pair on nitrogen, compresses to about 107 degrees. Water, with two lone pairs on oxygen, compresses further still to about 104.5 degrees. Three molecules, three central atoms from the same second period row of the periodic table, three different bond angles, all stemming from the exact same tetrahedral electron geometry and differing only in how many of the four domains are lone pairs rather than bonding pairs.

Ammonia's pyramidal shape is also directly responsible for its chemical personality. Because the molecule is not flat and not symmetric in the way a trigonal planar molecule would be, its bond dipoles do not cancel, making ammonia a polar molecule. More importantly, the lone pair sitting at the top of the pyramid, pointing away from the three hydrogens, is fully exposed and available to interact with other atoms. This exposed lone pair is exactly what allows ammonia to act as a base, accepting a proton to form the ammonium ion, and it is what allows nitrogen to form coordinate bonds in countless other chemical contexts. The shape and the chemistry are two views of the same underlying electron arrangement.
